Jails, unlike prisons, are mostly for people who have not had a trial yet.

This statistic doesn't tell us much, and really, it's what we should expect.

Generally, in the US criminal justice system, jail serves two roles:

  1. Pre-trial detention. This is where you go after booking when you're arrested for a crime. These prisoners are coming in right off the street, brought in by force against their will, and they may be accused of serious and/or violent crimes. These are your "not convicted of a crime" guys.

  2. Incarceration for short periods of time (less than a year or two max, usually a few months, depending on jurisdiction) for minor crimes. Failure to pay child support, multiple DUI's, minor drug offenses, petty theft, simple assault, etc. These prisoners are coming from a place of stability - they either self reported to jail as instructed or they were transferred from the above group after spending weeks or months incarcerated. These are your "have been convicted of a crime" guys. Real criminals go on to state prison.

Wouldn't you expect the vast majority of deaths in jail to be from group #1? Who's more likely to die in jail, a shit throwing biter who was dragged in at 3 in the morning after stabbing someone and is on who knows what cocktail of drugs, or the accounts payable guy who shows up to do his 30 days after getting his second DUI?

By the nature of things, of the prisoners in jail, the ones who have not been convicted of a crime are more unstable, violent, unpredictable, etc. than those who have. This statistic doesn't really tell us anything.
